procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 03.09.2008 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh, in Criminal Appeal No. 762-SB of 1998
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (convict accused) filed Criminal Appeal No. 762-SB of 1998 in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh, challenging the judgment and order of conviction passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Karnal. The High Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the conviction.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The convict accused approached the Supreme Court by filing Criminal Appeal No. 1722 of 2010, challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated 03.09.2008. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction.

directions: The appellant stands acquitted of the charge framed against him.

issue.issue_text: whether the High Court committed any error in passing the impugned judgment?

facts: The appellant was convicted by the Trial Court for the offence of abetment of suicide under Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code.
The High Court of Punjab & Haryana dismissed the appellant's appeal and affirmed the conviction.
The appellant then appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that there was no evidence of harassment to support the charge of abetment.
law: The case concerns the offence of abetment of suicide, punishable under Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code.
application: The Supreme Court considered the arguments from both the appellant and the State.
The appellant's counsel submitted that the lower courts erred as there was no evidence to suggest any harassment of the deceased by the appellant.
The State's counsel argued that the conviction was correct, emphasizing that the suicide occurred within seven years of the marriage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had committed an error. It allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the High Court that had affirmed the conviction, and acquitted the appellant of the charge.

issue.issue_text: Conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable u/s.306, Penal Code, 1860, if justified.

facts: A young woman, who was married to the appellant, committed suicide within seven years of the marriage.
The appellant had been demanding money from the deceased's parents to start a business.
The deceased was observed to be tense.
The Trial Court and the High Court convicted the appellant for abetment of suicide under Section 306 of the IPC based on these facts.
law: To establish guilt for abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC, the prosecution must provide cogent and convincing proof of an act of incitement that led to the suicide.
This act of incitement or offending action must be proximate in time to the commission of the suicide.
While factors like suicide occurring within seven years of marriage or demands for money are relevant, they are not sufficient on their own to prove abetment of suicide.
A conviction must be based on legal proof in accordance with the law, not on moral considerations.
application: The Supreme Court found that the lower courts had erred by failing to apply the correct legal principles for abetment of suicide.
The lower courts were overly influenced ("enamoured") by the facts that the suicide occurred within seven years of marriage, the appellant demanded money, and the deceased was tense.
The Court held that these circumstances, while relevant, did not meet the required legal standard for a conviction under Section 306 IPC.
Crucially, the evidence on record lacked the necessary "cogent and convincing proof of the act of incitement" that was "proximate to the time of occurrence."
Without proof of a direct act of incitement close to the time of death, the conviction was deemed unsustainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction of the appellant for abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC was not justified. The Court found that the evidence on record failed to establish a proximate act of incitement to suicide, which is a necessary ingredient for the offence. Consequently, the Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgments of the lower courts, and acquitted the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: whether the High Court committed any error in passing the impugned judgment?
appellant_arguments: The Courts below, including the High Court, committed an error in holding the appellant guilty of abetting the commission of suicide.
There is not an iota of evidence to suggest any kind of physical or mental harassment of the deceased by her husband.
respondent_arguments: The Courts below rightly held the appellant guilty of the alleged offence.
The oral evidence of witnesses PW-4 and PW-5 was well appreciated.
The conviction is supported by the presumption of abetment of suicide by a married woman under Section 113A of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

arguments.issue_text: Conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable u/s.306, Penal Code, 1860, if justified.
appellant_arguments: The conviction should be set aside as there is no evidence to even remotely suggest any kind of physical or mental harassment of the deceased by the appellant.
respondent_arguments: The conviction was justified and the appellant was rightly held guilty.
The State relied on Section 113A of the Indian Evidence Act, which allows for a presumption of abetment of suicide by a married woman.
The oral evidence of witnesses PW-4 and PW-5 was well appreciated by the lower courts.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court is not bound in law to infer that a person intended or foresaw a result of their actions solely because it was a natural and probable consequence; instead, the court must determine intent or foresight by referencing all evidence and drawing inferences that are proper in the circumstances.
obiter: The High Court has laid much emphasis on Section 113A of the Evidence Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution has not been able to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_tests_applied: In order to convict a person under Section 306 of the IPC there has to be a clear mens rea to commit the offence. Mere harassment is not sufficient to hold an accused guilty.
A person intends a consequence when he (1)foresees that it will happen if the given series of acts or omissions continue, and (2)desires it to happen.

The presumption of abetment under Section 113A of the Evidence Act is discretionary, as indicated by the words 'may presume', and should not be invoked from the mere fact of suicide within seven years of marriage unless cruelty is proven.
policy_considerations: From the mere fact of suicide within seven years of marriage, one should not jump to the conclusion of abetment unless cruelty was proved.
When considering the presumption under Section 113A of the Evidence Act, the court must take into account all the circumstances of the case which is an additional safeguard.
